extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English poetry; literary critics and creative writers studying poetic style
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging and producing English poetry, focused on qualities of language, versification, characterization, imagination, and faults illustrated by Shakespeare, Milton, Dryden, and Pope. Useful for critics, students, and poets assessing poetic excellence and defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneity and vividness of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Words appear 'struck out at a heat, on the spur of the occasion' and have 'all the truth and vividness which arise from an actual impression of the objects.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valued quality: language that seems immediately inspired by perception or feeling rather than contrived. Example: Shakespeare's impassioned passages. Anti-pattern: overwrought or laboured phrasing that loses immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of diction — the single true word
rubrics_metrics.description: In some authors (Shakspeare cited) 'any other word but the true one, is sure to be wrong.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the poem by whether substitutions dilute effect; example given where failing to recall 'Light thickens' would make suitable replacement unlikely. Guidance: prioritize striking, irreplaceable words that capture feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagistic / hieroglyphical language
rubrics_metrics.description: Language that 'translates thoughts into visible images' — words functioning as pictorial symbols rather than abstract statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for terse, image-rich phrasing that evokes sight/sensation. Shakespeare's epithets and phrases often work this way; they create immediate visual or sensory impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sudden transitions and elliptical expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent abrupt shifts and ellipses in phrasing are a stylistic trait, producing compressed, energetic speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These can cause mixed metaphors but have become idioms and contribute to force and rapidity. Anti-pattern: overuse that confuses rather than enlivens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance of mixed metaphor when idiomatic
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed metaphors in Shakespeare are 'only abbreviated forms of speech' and, by long use, 'have become idioms in the language.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a mixed metaphor feels organic and idiomatic (acceptable) or jarring and careless (fault). Consider reader familiarity and cumulative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate register for business/prose passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may use technical or affectated prose for official or conversational sections (example: Othello's senate apology vs official dispatches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess fit between register and dramatic situation; awkwardly archaic or affected official prose may be a flaw if it impedes clarity or verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versification variety and adaptability
rubrics_metrics.description: Versification that ranges 'from the ease and familiarity of measured conversation to the lyrical sounds' and is 'powerful, sweet, and varied.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prize blank verse (Shakespeare, Milton) that adapts sound and movement to sense — rising, falling, pausing as occasion requires. Anti-pattern: sing-song regularity or mechanical metre that mismatches content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability of blank verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Blank verse that is itself readable for its movement and musicality (Milton and Shakespeare singled out).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether blank verse reads as natural and musical rather than merely metrical; compare to other blank verse works (Thomson, Young, etc.) which may feel prosaic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and scope of imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: A genius that produces new, striking conceptions and images — 'epithets and single phrases are like sparkles, thrown off from an imagination, fired by the whirling rapidity of its own motion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure originality by the freshness of images and the poet's capacity to surprise; beware of mannerism or recycled conceits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy vs universality of genius (potential disadvantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'universality of his genius' can be a disadvantage to single works because variety of resources may divert from most effectual purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique whether a poet's wide-ranging talents dilute focus in a given piece. Anti-pattern: diffuse energy leading to lack of concentrated effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of care and revision vs facility
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors who write with ease and facility may be 'relaxed and careless in critical places' and set less value on their excellences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess signs of careful crafting and revision; facility of production can yield great moments but also slackness in detail (blunders in chronology, geography).

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement and seriousness of purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's seriousness — whether he writes 'for posterity' or for immediate popular approval — affects artistic choices (Shakespeare 'wrote for the great vulgar and the small').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the intended audience and whether seeking immediate effect compromised long-term excellence; seriousness of purpose often correlates with sustained ambition (Milton's labour vs Shakespeare's ease).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/political and religious fervour in imaginative work
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's religious zeal and patriotic/prophetic aims impregnate his imagination; his 'worship of the Muse' and devotion to 'a perfect commonwealth' shape his poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a strong ideological or devotional commitment enriches the poem's depth and unity or narrows it. Milton's dedication produced intense labour and high standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artfulness and learnedness integrated into imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton 'has borrowed more than any other writer' yet remains distinct; his learning 'has the effect of intuition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether erudition is assimilated into a vivid imaginative whole rather than showing as mere citation. Positive when learned material becomes vivid description (even of things read about).

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of descriptive vividness across senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to describe visible objects and sensory detail with 'palpableness and truth' even when based on books rather than direct observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for multisensory vividness (sight, sound, smell) and convincing detail; Milton's passages evoke sculpture-like figures and natural history accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musicality and prosodic intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: The ear for music, and the 'power of approximating the varieties of poetical to those of musical rhythm,' shaping line-sound to meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether lineation, rhythm, and sound reinforce sense; Milton's blank verse molds sound to image (lines rise/fall/pause appropriately). Anti-pattern: metrical patterns that obscure or contradict sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandeur and unity of character and passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry's interest may rest on 'the daring ambition and fierce passions' of central characters (e.g., Milton's Satan) and the account of paradisaical happiness and its loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether characters are endowed with sustained psychological and moral magnitude; the poem's emotional power often derives from such large-scale characterisation rather than episodic incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroic complexity in antagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation of an antagonist (Satan) as a 'most heroic subject' with ambition, fortitude, and complex mixture of pride and suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a villain is rendered with heroic scale and internal coherence — capable of pity and admiration as well as condemnation; such complexity enhances sublime effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathos of repose and contemplative emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain passages (Adam and Eve) derive power from repose, enjoyment, and contemplative pathos rather than action — 'the pathos is of that mild contemplative kind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value quiet, contemplative emotion when it suits subject-matter; absence of dramatic action need not indicate weakness if repose yields deep feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of subject to style (natural vs artificial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between 'natural' style (Chaucer, Spenser, Shakespeare, Milton) and 'artificial' style (Dryden, Pope); each aims at different faculties and audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether poet's chosen style fits subject and intended audience. Artificial style may excel at wit, elegance, and polish; natural style at impassioned imagination and spontaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical detachment and representation of common life
rubrics_metrics.description: Pope represents things 'as they appear to the indifferent observer' and can 'represent them in the most contemptible and insignificant point of view' (satire), or 'adorn the trivial incidents' with elegance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess effectiveness of satirical distance and elegance: is the mock-dignity apt and illuminating or merely petty? Value clarity of social observation and polish of expression.
